## Commit Placement (CP)

Promote a Placement Board's `draft` to its committed `placements`.

```ts
new CommitPlacementCommand(commandContext).execute({
  board,                    // linksTo PlacementBoard, required
  allowOverCapacity: false,
  committedByName: 'Alice',
})
```

Returns `{ placedCount, movedCount, removedCount, message }`.

### The single writer

This command is the **only** thing that writes `placements`. The board's UI touches `draft` and nothing else; no component in the family writes the committed field. That is what makes it safe to leave a half-finished plan open — the live arrangement cannot drift while someone is still dragging.

If a second writer is ever added, this guarantee is gone and the draft/commit split stops meaning anything.

### Two refusals

**Over capacity.** Refuses while any zone exceeds its ceiling, naming each one (`feature (3/2)`). The gate calls the same `overCapacityZones()` the board's header badge calls, so the UI can never promise a commit this will reject.

`allowOverCapacity` overrides it, because real arrangements do get squeezed — one extra chair at the family table. The override is opt-in and is written into the result message, so a commit that broke a stated ceiling is never silent.

**No-op.** Refuses when `draft` already matches `placements`, rather than writing an identical array and bumping the instance's index generation for nothing.

### The message describes the change, not the end state

`movedCount` and `removedCount` are computed from a before/after map built **before** the write. "12 placed" tells a reader nothing about what this commit did; "3 moved, 1 removed, 12 placed in total" does.

### Copy, don't alias

```ts
board.placements = draft.map((p) => p);
```

Assigning `draft` directly would make both fields the same array: the next edit to the draft would silently mutate what was just committed, and `hasUncommittedChanges` would never read true again. The board would look permanently clean while diverging from reality — a bug that is invisible until someone notices the plan on screen is not the plan that shipped.

### Comparison is normalised

Every item comparison goes through `itemKey()` (last two path segments), so a hand-authored board using `../Author/jane-doe` and a runtime card id of `https://…/my-realm/Author/jane-doe` are the same item. Without it the dirty check would fire on every load and `movedCount` would count every item as moved.

### Non-goals

Does not write to the placed items themselves — committing a seating plan does not stamp a `table` field onto each guest. If the arrangement needs to land on the records, that is a second command the host writes, and it should read `placements` after this one succeeds.

Does not check permissions, does not notify, does not snapshot the previous arrangement. A board that needs an undo history should keep its own.
